name: Animation from Interactions
explanation: Some user interactions, like scrolling, hovering, or clicking, trigger a motion animation. This could be a parallax effect or an element sliding, zooming, or spinning into view. When that happens, there needs to be a way to turn the animation off. The exception is when the motion itself is essential to what's being communicated, or to the function of the feature. A video editing timeline is one example, where the animation is the actual content, not a decorative effect layered on top of it.
whoItAffects: People with vestibular disorders can feel dizziness, nausea, or headaches from motion effects. Parallax scrolling and large zoom or slide transitions are common triggers, even without a rapid flash. People with attention-related disabilities can find animated transitions distracting too. This gets worse when the transitions show up often, as a side effect of ordinary scrolling. A setting to disable interaction-triggered animation lets these users browse in comfort, with full access to the content and the feature itself.
howToTest: Interact with the page the way a typical user would. Scroll through it, hover over elements, click buttons and links. Note any motion effects that trigger as a result, such as parallax backgrounds, sliding panels, zooming images, or animated transitions. Then turn on your operating system's reduce-motion setting and repeat the same interactions. The animations should be much reduced or removed, unless that motion is essential to the content or the task.

check.question: A marketing site uses a parallax scrolling effect where background images move at a different speed than foreground text as the user scrolls, purely for visual style. The site does not respect the operating system's reduced-motion setting and offers no other way to disable it. Does this pass SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions?
choices: Yes, because parallax scrolling is a common design trend
No, because the interaction-triggered animation isn't essential to the content and there's no way to disable it
Yes, because the effect only involves background images, not interactive controls
It depends only on how fast the user scrolls
